c-6c4effe620.text: The transfer to DIA was INSCOM's own recommendation, not a DIA rescue after a congressional petition. In July 1984 INSCOM's commanding general wrote that 'INSCOM ... should discontinue our involvement with psychoenergetic research and operations', intended 'to cease INSCOM CENTER LANE Project operations on 30 Sept 1984', and asked for authority to permit 'timely and undisrupted transfer of (1) ICLP operations to a national agency such as DIA or NSA'. The letter of 2 March 1985 then notified HQDA of 'the deactivation of the INSCOM CENTER LANE Project, the attachment OPCON of CENTER LANE assets and resources to the Defense Intelligence Agency, and the retirement of CENTER LANE as an active project nickname'. Nothing opened mentions Vorona or a petition to Congress.

claimed.text: Joseph McMoneagle has described his own route into the programme as a chain of individual postings and reassignments by generals, ending with an abrupt order to look at GRILL FLAME at SRI.
Kit Green says that at CIA he was the officer to whom anomalous-phenomena reporting was routed, and he is described as CIA's monitor for the SRI work.
James Clapper, later Director of National Intelligence, is recorded as a project leader of the programme in the 1990s.
Jacques Vallee, at SRI in the early 1970s in the same period as Puthoff's programme, is said to have been consulted on the classified remote-viewing research.

contested.text: Several common accounts do not survive the documents: the CENTER LANE office was the Security Support Detachment, not the Systems Exploitation Detachment; the move to DIA was INSCOM's own recommendation, not a DIA rescue after a congressional petition; and the 1995 review was the CIA's, not the veterans'.

The board reads STAR GATE as the closest documented analogue to the concealment structure it alleges for materiel exploitation, contractor science inside compartmented military operations, and DIA's decades running it as the precedent for its 2008 AAWSAP contract. These are structural inferences.
The board holds that a ridiculed subject was carried at service-secretary level of access control, but notes that no opened record connects CENTER LANE to waived or unacknowledged status.

The board infers that the consciousness framing entered the modern UAP programmes through personnel continuity rather than evidence, carried by Puthoff, Green and Vallee across both eras, and that four decades of funding for one investigator show a durable requirement.
The board infers that the repeated renaming shows codeword churn on compromise is standard practice, which is why searches of the UAP record by programme name under-count.

lead.text: STAR GATE is the last name of the US government's remote-viewing effort. CIA's Office of Technical Service funded research by Harold Puthoff and Russell Targ at SRI from 1972, and the work ran under federal contract through Army and DIA programmes until 1995, when a CIA-commissioned evaluation found the information too vague and ambiguous for actionable intelligence and the programme was ended.

record.text: INSCOM dates its own psychoenergetics work from Project GRILL FLAME in 1977 and says the project was run on an ad hoc basis, with resources taken out of hide.

A 1978 talking paper records the Army's intelligence chief and INSCOM's commander agreeing that INSCOM would check out parapsychology and that Army Intelligence would obligate $75,000 for an SRI subject selection and training programme, with orientation at SRI in November 1978.

INSCOM's FY1981 history records that GRILL FLAME began as a specially controlled and compartmented activity under the Army's intelligence chief, that INSCOM was orally tasked to evaluate it in October 1978, and that programme management passed to INSCOM's Detachment G on 11 February 1981.

The CENTER LANE project office was the Security Support Detachment of the 902d Military Intelligence Group at Fort Meade. Its programme package proposed a new intelligence programme using psychoenergetics and records taskings from 1978 to 1983 for the Army, DIA, the Joint Chiefs, CIA, NSA, the FBI and the Secret Service.

Every page of CENTER LANE's paperwork carries a special access warning restricting it to those with category three access, and its deactivation letter asks the Army to discontinue it as a Secretary of the Army designated special access programme. Its security classification guide is indexed but withheld.

INSCOM's commanding general wrote in July 1984 that the command should end its involvement in psychoenergetic research and operations and transfer them to a national agency such as DIA or NSA; the letter of 2 March 1985 records the deactivation and the attachment of CENTER LANE assets to DIA.
A 1985 memorandum recommending a twelve-person prototype operational group gives the SUN STREAK budget line as DRAGOON ABSORB.

An INSCOM memorandum of 9 June 1983 assesses the Monroe Institute's Gateway Experience for personnel required to take the training, names remote viewing as a follow-on technique within it, and finds a sound basis for considering it plausible, while recording that the Institute's own trainers said no one had ever read all ten numbers correctly in out-of-body tests.

The 1995 evaluation, An Evaluation of Remote Viewing: Research and Applications, was written for the American Institutes for Research by Michael Mumford, Andrew Rose and David Goslin, with Jessica Utts and Ray Hyman as reviewers. It found the information vague and ambiguous, never used to guide intelligence operations, and concluded that continued operational use was not warranted.
The review was the CIA's own, run by its Office of Research and Development with the AIR panel, and a CIA paper of June 1995 records the choice of an outside panel as deliberate strategy.
The released records withhold the unit's people: session forms leave the remote viewer, interviewer and observer fields blank, and memoranda substitute CIA release codes for names.

summary.text: Secondary accounts give the effort a succession of cryptonyms: SCANATE at CIA around 1970, GONDOLA WISH in 1977, GRILL FLAME from 1978, CENTER LANE from 1983, SUN STREAK at DIA from late 1985 and STAR GATE from 1991. The opened records confirm GRILL FLAME, CENTER LANE and SUN STREAK becoming STAR GATE, and add a budget-line name, DRAGOON ABSORB.

SRI held the science half. Puthoff and Targ published remote-viewing results in Nature in October 1974 and wrote the Standard Remote Viewing Protocol of November 1978, later declassified; CIA's Office of Technical Service funded the work from 1972 before Army INSCOM and DIA took over sponsorship.

The Army staff started the operational side: Army Intelligence paid for SRI to select and train INSCOM personnel in 1978, GRILL FLAME passed to INSCOM in 1981, and its successor CENTER LANE was a Secretary of the Army designated special access programme until INSCOM recommended ending it in 1984 and handed its assets to DIA in 1985.

At the end the DIA programme was three remote viewers and three support staff. The American Institutes for Research evaluation of September 1995 closed it, and the CIA put the records online in its CREST archive in January 2017.

The same principal investigator links this programme to the later UAP work: Puthoff ran the SRI science, was hired as a consultant by Bigelow's NIDS, wrote a reference document under AAWSAP and co-founded To The Stars Academy.
